Best book I’ve ever played. Seriously, there is no way back, once you start this journey you will either love it or you didn’t finish it, there is no in between.
All you have to know is that you have to read a lot, enormously a lot, like a lot. The game is like 85% reading, so make sure you are truly committed to this journey.
I have to admit I have never imagined I would enjoy this game so much, despite the game being made in 1999 it’s still worth playing even today. 
The story is complicated, at first you won’t understand ♥♥♥♥, but slowly you will get to *know* the interesting nature of this world. Trying to figure it out what happened, why it happened, and connecting all the information you get through speaking to random strangers is quite fun.
Your decisions matter, your choices matter. Trust whoever you want or stab them in the back because you think they deserved it. Every interaction feels important and it is indeed important, the game appreciates your curiosity if you check every dialogue option.
Your companions' personalities are just so entertaining, I started to care about their well being, and it affected me deeply. I will remember them fondly, they helped me, they trusted me even though they didn’t have to. 
Overall, I had a great experience and gained some great wisdom through the game.

Изначально я решил попробовать эту игру только потому, что ждал чего-то в духе диско элизиум. На поверхности сходства и правда есть - главный герой, потерявший память, попытка узнать своё прошлое и ответы на вопросы, необходимость разговаривать почти с каждым нпс. Но на деле оказалось что геймплейно это вообще другая игра и ждать от неё прямого сходства с диско не стоит.
Как я и сказал, сюжет строится вокруг Безымянного, который пытается понять кто он такой и что с ним произошло. Лор здесь интересный, игра поначалу затрагивает темы жизни и смерти, но продвинувшись чуть дальше оказывается что это было малой частью того что есть в Сигиле. В каждом регионе есть свои конфликты и фракции и по сюжету Безымянному придется в них вступать чтоб узнать о себе. Особенно круто, что прошлое всплывает не только в основных заданиях, но и в побочных квестах - они лучше раскрывают Безымянного и мир.
Был даже момент, когда я не мог выполнить один квест, не завершив другой, и это добавляет игре ощущение связности, хотя подобных пересечений здесь не так много.
Боевая система мне не понравилась. В начале она сводится к закликиванию, а разнообразие появляется начиная с середины игры, когда появляются новые напарники и заклинания. Не понравилось техническое состояние игры. Один раз я застрял в лабиринте Рейвел из-за того, что катсцена не проигрывалась до конца, проблему удалось решить только сменой языка на польский. Игра в принципе довольно сложновата, порой без правильной последовательности в диалогах и еще каких-то обстоятельств ты не можешь использовать тот или иной предмет, из-за чего приходится прибегать к гайдам

Planescape Torment is a strange beast. To approach it now as I am, after having only dipped my pinkies into the more literary side of gaming, was a real challenge that I had to push through. Claiming that it's "rough around the edges" would be putting it mildly: Planescape Torment is barely functional at times and the more you delve into its story, the more you're likely to have it ruined by some monumental idiocy of game design. After 60 hours of playing it in the most by the rules ways I could manage, I still found myself forced to pull out the wiki from the internet, lower the difficulty out of sheer frustration, and then almost drop the game entirely right before I got to the ending because Planescape seemed hellbent on trying to soft-lock me in a definitive way at every turn. In fact, I can count myself lucky to have gotten to the ending myself because if I had just a tiny bit less resources or if I didn't finish some specific and easily missed questlines, then I wouldn't have been able to: this is the frailty of this videogame's balance. Not to mention that I installed not one, but two mods before starting the adventure specifically to avoid cases like this!
A charitable read on my part would put it in the context of its era. This videogame is older than me, after all, and my inexperience with classic RPGs like it leaves me without a meter of comparison. Even in terms of graphics, I wouldn't be able to tell you if what I saw on screen was impressive for the time or already aged on arrival. What it is worth discussing, though, is the most immortal part of itself: the story it tells and the way it does so.
From the very first moments of gameplay, Planescape sets a standard for its narration. They're dark and bloody, but also filled with irony and in open subversion to classic DnD tropes, all of it tinged with a hint of existentialism that could only grow through time. The Mortuary also introduces you to the factions of Sigil and some of its most compelling worldbuilding aspects, quickly letting you get full control of exploration in the City of Portals itself. Sigil will be the center piece of most od what the game has to offer: it's a place I have come to slowly know, love and even miss (we'll get to that...). It's one of constant trade, where a number of races, factions and ideologies constantly collide with one another in a way that takes full inspiration from DnD's alignment system. Lawful good, chaotic neutral, neutral evil... these are the moral terms through which Planescape's world functions, and while they might seem simple at first, the worldbuilding manages to give them any interesting turn. Sigil, just like our Nameless One, is both all of them together and not one of them at any single time: an entity that has a very definite identity, but that also presents many faces inside itself. Piles of mechanical garbage, houses made of rocks and rusted iron, all edges and no dull surfaces... Sigil's architecture reflects the harshness of its environment, which is filled with thugs and thiefs behind every corner. For the city of Portals, a place everyone would like to conquer due to its peculiar position between the planes, it looks rather understated, which I also liked. The game doesn't aim to get you through pyrotechnics or incredible set pieces, and lacking the technical prowess to do so, it focuses a lot on art direction. Sigil is off-putting in a fascinating way, it became very dear to me because of that; just as much as that off-putting nature helps to build upon its esotericism, with the rich descriptions of the ways to open its Portals for example.
The setting being ripped out of classic DnD is a doubled-edged sword. It lays a stable foundation for what's to come, between demons, witches, planes and planewalkers; but at the same time, it can also muddle the waters. A prime example would be the way people die in Sigil: based on the lore explained to you, it seems to me that being effectively immortal and having your soul be recycled to the Blood War after having its memory wiped is either the natural way of things or very common, at the very least. Planescape is at its best when it's entirely about the city and the literal deja-vu TNO has when he wanders through a place he both doesn't know and that he has been a citizen of for centuries, leaving deep marks of his passage. That's what's the most interesting feature of Planescape's story, and that's also why I came to it in the first place. It is widely known as the main game that inspired Disco Elysium and it's obvious as soon as you begin: Harry and TNO are both amnesiac and they're both confronted with the actions of their own past selves in a city that keeps inspiring impressions, memories and even political opinions in them. Planescape's writing isn't as evocative as Disco Elysium's, being much more in line with the tone of a dungeon master, but it is nonetheless inspired, rich and filled to the brim with different dialects. Without the voice acting that gives a specific tone to its characters, Planescape opts for very peculiar ways of speaking in order to breathe life into its most important characters. Morte's wiseacre jokes due to his ironic detachment from his sorry condition, Fall-from-Grace's silvery tongue and excellent persuasion, Annah's nigh incomprehensible accent, Dakkon's way of *knowing* things, Ignus' fiery derangement and Mordon's beep-boopistic computer speech: I ended up loving the small party of freaks the game gradually builds up for you, in a way which was organic, even if a bit unbalanced. Instead of having your standard helpers who fulfill a role for combat more than anything else, the companions of TNO are people with often profound stories about them. Uncovering them all was one of the best things about the game, even when they slogged down the progress of the wider story.
This would be a nice place to address the misogynistic elephant in the room. Planescape doesn't have the same kind of misogyny which you would expect from a game of its day and age, but it nonetheless suffers from a very stereotyped and sometimes quite judgmental way of writing its female characters. The hints of it can be found early on, between Morte's inappropriate jokes about female ghouls (they can be funny the first time, but they are repeated so many times that you start finding it insane that you're supposed to find Morte endearing by that point) and some of the descriptions of the bestiary. Also, the limited graphics hide it well, but the character design of so many of the female characters is either: 1) old lady, or 2) busty sex doll that *wants* you. This is then propedeutic to the realisation I had when I considered that before the halfway point in the story the only characters of note were all male, while the only female companion by then was incredibly shallow and defined by her immediate infatuation to you. Oh, and the past female companion, Deionarra, is also defined by her undying and almost obsessive love for you. Fall-from-Grace makes things better, but even there the most flirty interactions hurt my soul in a way a night hag's spell would never be able to. This is the kind of culture which the rpgs which turn your party into an harem stem stem from, but in Planescape it rings even more hollow by virtue of comparison. The game has consistently so much to say and with such quality about the human condition that it's ironic when it somehow goes back to seeing women as either objects of desire or entirely dependant on their romantic impulses.
This is unfortunately the one note of reprimand I have for Ravel, the climax of Planescape as a whole...

[b]Wieloświat.[/b]
Planescape: Torment to gra cRPG, stworzona przez Black Isle Studios, i wydana dzięki Interplay Entertainment w 1999 roku.
Aczkolwiek...
Planescape to nie sztampowe fantasy. To studium natury człowieka. To kosmologia. Wieloplanarne uniwersum osadzone w multiwersum Dungeons & Dragons, w którym każda sfera istnienia jest jednocześnie miejscem i filozoficznym argumentem. W samym sercu tego chaosu leży Sigil - Miasto Drzwi. Paradoksalne metropolia zawieszona na szczycie nieskończonego cyklu, rządzona przez tajemniczą Panią Bólu, niedostępna dla nikogo. Potężna i przerażająca ponad innych bogów. Ta która karze swoich wyznawców i zabrania w siebie wierzyć.
Zaś samo Sigil to miejsce, gdzie spotykają się wszystkie płaszczyzny, a każda uliczka niesie inną teologię. Tutaj środowisko nie jest tłem. Jest rozmówcą.
W tym świecie budzimy się jako Bezimienny - istota pokryta bliznami, tatuażami i zapiskami zostawionymi przez poprzednie wcielenia samego siebie. W niezmierzonym cyklu śmierci i wskrzeszeń. Ścigany przez cienie i demony. Obarczony niewybaczalnym czynem i gwałtem na egzystencji poprzez eksperymenty z nieśmiercą.
Nieśmiertelny. Niepamiętający. Zagubiony. I właśnie ta zagubiona tożsamość staje się osią całego dzieła. Nie ratujemy świata, nie szukamy potęgi. Szukamy odpowiedzi na pytanie: kim jesteśmy? A głębiej - czy to, czym byliśmy, musi określać to, czym możemy się stać?

[b]"Przed wyruszeniem w drogę..."[/b]
Towarzysze tej podróży to postacie tak wyraziste, że każda zasługuje na osobny esej.
*Morte - latająca czaszka z jadowitym językiem i sercem cięższym, niż chciałby przyznać.
*Nie-Sława - sukkub prowadząca Zamtuz Rozkoszy Zmysłowych, filozofka, której opanowanie jest głębsze niż jakakolwiek ekstaza.
*Nordom - modron wygnany z Mechanicznego Ula za to, że zaczął zadawać pytania. 
*Dak’kon - githzerai dźwigający ciężar przysięgi złożonej komuś, kogo już nie ma. 
Każda z nich niesie własną wersję pytania z tytułu. Każda jest inną, niepełną, bolesną odpowiedzią. A to zaledwie kilkoro z nie-wymienionych kompanów, których drogi splotły się z Bezimiennym.

[b]"Pióro jest silniejsze od miecza."[/b]
Mechaniki RPG istnieją tu wbrew konwencji gatunku.
Walka jest możliwa, ale w dużej mierze opcjonalna. Gra znacznie hojniej nagradza mądrość, perswazję i pamięć niż ostrze. Wiele konfliktów da się rozwiązać słowem. Niektórych wrogów można zbawić. Innych - i to jest jeden z najodważniejszych pomysłów w historii gier - pokonać, rozumiejąc ich lepiej, niż oni rozumieją samych siebie. Statystyki mają znaczenie, lecz prawdziwą wagę niosą wybory: moralne, filozoficzne, egzystencjalne.
Gra pyta, jakim wcieleniem chcemy być - i pamięta każdy nasz krok.

[b]Turpizm i surrealizm.[/b]
Szata audiowizualna nie próbuje rywalizować z czasem, w którym powstała. Zamiast tego tworzy własny, niepowtarzalny język - każda lokacja jest starannie skomponowanym obrazem i onirycznym nastrojem, często zahaczając artyzmem o obrazy H.R.Gigera czy Zdzisława Beksińskiego.
Dzielnica Ula gnije w brunatnych tonach biedy i rezygnacji, Kamienica Zbójców lśni chłodnym dostojeństwem, a Śmieciowe Labirynty oddychają klaustrofobią. Muzyka Marka Morgana to absolutnie osobny rozdział: ambientowa, dysharmonijna, melancholijna, wpełzająca pod skórę. Utwory takie jak Smoldering Corpses czy Curst nie ilustrują świata - są jego emocjonalnym rdzeniem.

[b]Literatura - Głupcze ![/b]
Lecz największym, absolutnym centrum grawitacji jest tekst. Bowiem tytuł zawiera więcej przemyślanych słów i literackiej finezji niż niejedna powieść. Dialogi nie przekazują informacji -  filozofują, prowokują, uwodzą i kaleczą. Opisy lokacji to miniatury prozatorskie. Gra mówi o śmierci jak o starym znajomym, o bólu jak o nauczycielu, o tożsamości jak o polu bitwy, z którego nie można uciec. Sztuka piśmiennicza ze spikselowanych marzeń.

[b]Jedyna w swoim rodzaju.[/b]
Inne gry mają filozofię. Planescape: Torment jest filozofią.
To różnica, której nie można zbagatelizować. Można wskazać dziesiątki tytułów, które podejmują Wielkie Pytania - Disco Elysium pyta o politykę i tożsamość, Nier: Automata o sens istnienia, Spec Ops: The Line o moralność przemocy. Wszystkie robią to dobrze. Niektóre - znakomicie. Ale niemal każda z nich używa filozofii jako narzędzia narracyjnego: jako wzmocnienia fabuły.
Torment robi coś innego. Tu filozofia jest fabułą. Jest mechaniką. Jest światem, postaciami, dialogiem i ciszą między słowami. Jest matematyką świata i jego organiką - myślą, rzeczywistością, zamysłem i niewyobrażalnym.
Każda rozmowa z NPC, każdy opis przedmiotu w ekwipunku, każda, walka, rozmowa i decyzja dotycząca tego, kim chcemy być - wszystko to jest gestem głęboko filozoficznym.

[b]"Oto jest pytanie."[/b]
 I tak wracamy do pytania, które gra stawia z uporem filozofa i siłą poety:
Co może zmienić naturę człowieka?
Planescape: Torment nie daje jednej ostatecznej odpowiedzi. 
Sugeruje, że może to zrobić ból - choć nie zawsze. Że miłość - lecz czasem tylko odsłania to, co już w nas było. Że śmierć - ale Bezimienny wraca, czasem taki sam, czasem inny. Pokazuje, że natura człowieka nie jest kamieniem, lecz rzeką: płynącą, zmienną, niepowtarzalną.
...

[b]A może odpowiedzią jest samo pytanie?[/b]
Gotowość, by je zadać.
Odwaga, by nie odwrócić wzroku.
Gra zadaje je raz po raz - z każdej blizny, z każdego strzępku pamięci, z każdej śmierci i każdego powrotu. A gdy kończysz, patrzy ci w oczy i milczy, zostawia Cię z Twoją własną, niełatwą odpowiedzią.
I w tej ciszy - jeśli jesteś gotów/gotowa ją usłyszeć - brzmi jedyna odpowiedź, która ma znaczenie: Ty sam/sama.
Dlatego właśnie Planescape: Torment jest - Arcydziełem.

Back when this game was released originally, I couldn't make myself play it. I tried once, but the game has been too slow, I disliked the setting, and I absolutely could not stand the fact that I am unable to create my own character.

26 years later, I have finally decided to give it another shot, this time in the Ehnanced version. I haven't met a single person who disliked this game, and everyone was always in shock how I skipped such a gem and a groundbreaking game of that era. So I said to myself I'm going to complete it even if I do not like it.

I'm aware this will be immediately stigmatized by the numerous fans, but I still retain most of my negative impressions of the game, and I must admit I did not enjoy the game so much, all until the end, and that final chapter.

You see, this game has as its strongest points, one of the most memorable storylines I have ever seen in gaming, and probably one of the best story conclusions to this day. I'm under the impression that it would have been better if this was a book, than a game. I still disliked the character progression and the lack of liberty to create a character as I like it. But this is not the point of this game. I disliked the many "fetch" side quests. I'm still not a fan of the setting and the many planes of D&D multiverse. But the main plot, its narrative, its twists and especially the ending really oblige me to say that despite everything this game is worth playing, and I have to say it is a classic that should be played by every RPG fan out there, and the game is justifiably praised by so many. I'd still say it does not deserve so much hype, but it definitely deserves all the praise its getting to this day.

BioWare’s infinite engine shows its age; pathfinding is especially cumbersome, even compared to other games from the same year, like Diablo. Melee combat is sometimes frustrating, and spell animations are meh (again, compared to Diablo).

On the other hand, the game is a solid implementation of 2nd Ed AD&D Rules and the Planescape campaign setting; the lore is introduced beautifully through factions, NPCs and locations. The artwork, music and voice acting add a lot to the game immersion. As a D&D DM who played AD&D back in the day and now narrates a D&D 5th edition Planescape Campaign, this game is a must.

It’s important to clarify that this is not a combat-focused action RPG, it's a story-focused, dialogue-heavy RPG, where every dialogue decision counts, because it's important for you, for the story, and for the party if you choose to be good/neutral/evil, and lawful/neutral/chaotic. 

You can lie or tell the truth, do something for free, or charge for it. You can vow to do something and later betray a companion; most powerful quest reward items are restricted to these decisions. Decisions and their impact in the story are the most important aspect of the game (not damage/combat), this is why WIS/INT/CHA are the most important stats, you can run away from 99% of the fights, or solve them through dialogue, and if you die, you just come back to life.

This lead us to the best attribute of the game, storytelling. Oh, men, what can I say? It’s an existentialist masterpiece. You wake up in the mortuary, without memories,  realise that you are immortal, and begin a quest across the planes to figure out the puzzle of your memory, your past lives, and your immortality. It’s something between Memento, Fight Club, Inception, and Eternal Sunshine of a Spotless Mind.

I totally recommend this if you want an engaging existentialist story.

Planescape Torment has a cult following for a reason. I cannot recommend it enough.

This game can be used as a philosophy handbook (though mostly existential). It asks huge questions even in seemingly unimportant conversations. The world is built as a representation of different ideas, the core of it being the fact that *belief* can change reality.

The Nameless One doesn't just represent someone going through the story, but shaping the story through your *beliefs*. It can be a direct implementation of your moral codex, challenged throughout the game.

It requests your full attention, and *If* you are ready for it, it will reward you like no other.  

Philosophy handbook clarification. I will go over a few points.
- Torment. "The meaninglessness of suffering, not suffering itself, was the curse that lay over mankind so far", Nietzsche. Can we give meaning to your suffering? Or will we suffer under its meaninglessness?
- Duty. Do you stay stay true to your word, or do you bend reality to fit your needs? Would you betray in order to gain something, or do what is right for the sake of that it is right. This is Kantian deontology at its core, questioning if the morality of an action is tied to the consequences of it, or rather is it moral in question to a set of rules.
- TNO starts as a blank slate, you have no meaning and have a chance to make it. "Existence precedes essence", Sartre.
- "What can change the nature of a man?" is a sort of meta-question for the progression of the character. It is asked at different points of the game, and, if the player is reflecting, can have different answers. Answering it can deepen your relation to evolution and self-overcoming (Nietzsche). Is identity continuous, or are we built by a sequence of different *selves* tied together by consequence?
- "Endure, in enduring grow strong", Dak'kon. Central to self-overcoming.
- The City of Doors is not simply a place with portals, but an implementation of worlds within worlds. This highlights the theme of existentialism which stands by individual experience as the core principle. Struggling through it, you are trying to make yourself once more.
This game changed my life when I first played in all those years ago.

[code]While not all components of Planescape: Torment have aged well in the 25+ years since its original release, it remains a great game for players who prefer role-playing games with a focus on dialogue instead of combat, offering an delightfully strange and atmospheric tale set in one of D&D’s most famous cities[/code]

Among the games that are based on the Infinity Engine, which mostly brought the [i]Dungeons & Dragons[/i] 2e ruleset to life, [i]Baldur’s Gate I & II[/i] (1998, 2000) remain the most popular to this day and are usually credited as all-time classics whose influence shaped roleplaying-games as a whole. In contrast, [i]Planescape: Torment[/i] (1999) is usually described as a less approachable package due to its focus on dialogue instead of combat – as well as being set in the comparatively bizarre [i]Planescape[/i] setting of [i]Dungeons & Dragons[/i], rather than the straightforward [i]Forgotten Realms[/i]. However, by focussing on the narrative aspects of roleplaying-games, [i]Torment[/i] has emerged as a popular recommendation for players who would rather exchange words with NPCs than blows – and while it’s usually only ranked as the third-most popular Infinity Engine game, [i]Torment[/i] has thus gained a cult following on its own.

Now, this review does not aim to draw up detailed comparisons between [i]Torment[/i] and the other Infinity Engine games, as doing so would not be adequately possible in this format. Yet, the legacy of [i]Torment[/i] is important to mention, as it already showcases the game’s strength – putting its narrative above everything else – as well as its weakness – being less well-rounded in other aspects as a consequence. Especially thanks to the passage of time, more than 25 years since its original release, [i]Torment[/i] does suffer from a lot of gameplay-related issues, from a weak combat system to a clunky user interface, which do diminish the overall experience. However, the actual writing – an enthralling setting, memorable characters, exciting plot developments and decisions that actually affects progression – still manages to shine through, turning [i]Torment[/i] into the enjoyable experience that’s still worth playing today, even if it may take a bit of getting used-to.

Speaking of, considering this current version of [i]Torment[/i] was released by BeamDog in 2017, eighteen years after the original, one may wonder if it received an overhaul to the degree of feeling like a modern cRPG. Unfortunately, while it does have become the best way to play the game today – along with the [url= https://www.pcgamingwiki.com/wiki/Planescape:_Torment_Enhanced_Edition#Essential_improvements]Unfinished Business mod[/url] for additional improvements – it’s important to note that most enhancements pertain to technical upgrades (bug fixes, UI resolution scaling, remastered soundtrack, etc.) and a few gameplay improvements (such as tab highlighting, area zooming or a quick loot function). As such, this version of the game should be treated as a way to easily make the game available on modern platforms, rather than a rework with the goal of modernising the contents themselves.

Naturally, with most of [i]Torment[/i] remaining untouched in terms of design, a cRPG from 1999 does not offer the same comfort as modern role-playing games do. In particular, even getting familiar with the different game mechanics can prove tough, as the game initial guidance for new players is lacking: Although a new “Help Overlay” button was added in the “Enhanced Edition” and there’s a [url= https://steamcdn-a.akamaihd.net/steam/apps/466300/manuals/PSTEE_Manual-v1.1.pdf?t=1572456225]12-page manual[/url] available online, these can’t make up for the complexity of the underlying [i]Dungeons & Dragons[/i] 2e ruleset on their own. Chances are high that those already interested in this game are familiar enough with the genre to be able to make it past the beginning – but for players without previous cRPG experience, this is not a great starting point.

Even if you can get past the initial hurdles however, the gameplay of [i]Torment[/i] still leaves a lot to be desired. While the necessary cRPG elements are all in place, as expected from an Infinity Engine game, [i]Torment[/i] does not offer much more than that. From the questionable pathfinding to the protagonist-centred level-up and obstruse class switching process, unnecessary inventory management and the clunky combat, not to mention the cumbersome user interface, there’s simply a lot of room left for improvement – especially when viewed from a modern perspective, taking the quality-of-life developments made in the genre during the past 25 years into account. While the gameplay [i]Torment[/i] never reaches the territory of being actively annoying or even entirely unplayable, it simply isn’t good enough (anymore?) to warrant a playthrough on its own, compared to the competition.

Age has been more kind to the narrative aspects of the game – while some dialogue trees could’ve been more streamlined and the overall text formatting improved (maybe through an option allowing for full-screen text rather than small dialogue boxes?), the setting, characters, plot and dialogues are definitely still worth a look today. Even after all these years – and a lot more undead protagonists in videogames, for example – [i]Torment[/i] still manages to craft a surprisingly complex tale around it’s undying hero and his unique companions, constantly questioning the nature of men and death itself.

[i]Torment[/i] has been called a “philosophical game” quite often and while there are certainly a lot of philosophical themes to be encountered, it also needs to be mentioned that they’re still part of a personal story, woven into the journey of an amnesiac undead trying to regain his memories in a strange city of different factions and species, pouring in from constantly changing portals. Don’t expect [i]Torment[/i] to be a straightforward lecture in philosophy – it’s a lengthy fantasy story with interesting questions and scenarios to be pondered on, seamlessly integrated into the main plot as well as optional side quests. In particular, it’s a worthwhile virtual novel for fans of deep worldbuilding, excessive but lore-heavy dialogues offering multiple consequences, and a story that keeps gaining layers and rewards those who always pay attention.

That said, even the writing is not without its faults. As typical for role-playing games, pacing is an issue, as [i]Torment[/i] can quickly devolve into hours of side-questing before the main plot comes into reach again. In addition, the first half of the game appears much more realised than the second half, which becomes a lot more streamlined and almost skips through some of the events that now take place. Furthermore, [i]Torment[/i] feels almost entirely devoid of party interaction, as the companions mostly interact with the protagonist but not with each other.

Still, even with its apparent edges and the unfortunate effects of ageing, [i]Torment[/i] remains a great choice for everyone who prefers story and dialogues in cRPGs over combat, a bizarre scenario over classic fantasy and slow but rewarding worldbuilding over a straightforward plot. With its competition constantly increasing over the years, it may not always be counted among the best-written RPG anymore, but with a bit of effort it still remains an incredibly enjoyable experience to this day.

The reason I wanted to play this game was because of it's philosophical exploration into the meaning of nature and existence. On that front it succeeds heavily, and I would say it's deserving of all the praise it's received. 

[spoiler] Initial reflections upon completing the game, the central theme is compelling. "What can change the nature of a man?" When I was first posed this question by Ravel, my response was death. It makes sense to me that when presented with the ultimate erasure of ones ego, one will go to great lengths to prevent such an outcome. This is reflected throughout the game, and I've noticed this pattern within my own life. However I also feel that love is a very strong motivator as well. Reflected within the games companions (which are all very well written characters), at the end where their love for TNO causes them to die at the hands of his mortality. Powerful stuff, and also something I've seen reflected in my own life. Obviously not to such a dramatic extent, but in pondering what this games philosophy is asking of you, that is the current conclusion I reach at this time in my life. 

The Nameless one is enough of a blank slate in this incarnation, and the game does a very good job of allowing the player to imprint themselves upon him, while still sticking to the rails of the games overarching story. As such, it's clear that Planescape: Torment is asking the player to internally reflect on these questions themselves, which then manifest within the game. Powerful stuff. Intriguing mysteries, with very well written characters, and satisfying outcomes. The ending of TNO fighting in the blood war after regaining his mortality is also really badass. [/spoiler]

On the other hand, this is THE most 90s CRPG I've ever played, in that it embodies all of the very valid frustrations that come with that specific era and genre of games. Which to be clear, I have a deep love and nostalgia for, but even a lot of what is presented here was frustrating to me. The combat mechanics are not good. I think this kind of game would have faired a lot better with some sort of turn based combat system. Admittedly I'm not a fan of real time strategy games at all, because I suck at them, but it was made more tolerable by the ability to pause combat. Still, in my opinion it was a slog putting up with to get to the parts I wanted to see.

A substantial handful of puzzles and points of progression are barred behind ridiculously esoteric solutions akin to that of some of the point and click puzzles of the 90s. Because of course you have to hide the banana behind the statue and wait 90 seconds, then squish it with your elbow which will summon bofus the spirit guide who will ask you 16 obscure riddles, that will give you a vague hint as to what it is you're supposed to do next. What are you stupid? How could you not figure that out?

Needless to say, I would recommend trying to play through as blindly as possible until you reach these points, in which case I would suggest just searching for the most specific and bare minimum pointers you need to progress. This worked very well for me, and I surprisingly avoided all major spoilers along the way. 
Also level INT and WIS because if you level anything else you've basically ruined your character. Fighter is completely useless in this game, unless you want to play "touch em a little bit and go + 10,000 bandages" simulator.

Let's say you'll come across a blue stone at the certain point, the literature, nothing ever compares!

If you're more of a modern gamer, like me, curb your expectations for a high fidelity combat system akin to BG3 or the Divinity games. This plays like more of a combat-lite "point-and-click adventure novel" with a heavy lore focus. To be honest, this is a game for DnD players, and that's kind of my favorite thing about it. It does a great job of introducing the player to the Planescape setting if all you've ever been exposed to is the Forgotten Realms or Greyhawk, etc. The combat is, however, very dated. Once you get a handle on it, though, the combat is genuinely reasonably satisfying (spacebar is pause, you can perform actions in pause mode and unpause to execute. PLEASE do this. lol). Talk to uniquely named NPCs, and even the apparently generic ones. If you want an optimal experience, try to start with as much INT and WIS as you can, even if you're playing fighter, because some of the better dialogue options are locked behind a good INT/WIS score. Your mages (namely Dak'kon) can supplement your STR at early levels with spells like Power of One to make your hits a little more effective, but there's also the option of playing a mage if you're into that (this is based on 2e, I think, so no cantrips, which is why I skipped on mage aside from swapping to cast "Friends" for a CHR buff). Look for secrets everywhere. Super excited for Blizzard in Baator!

Planescape: Torment — це питання: What can change the nature of a man?

Вона працює не механіками, а історією. Читати доведеться багато. Інколи текст надто багатослівний, бойова система відчутно застаріла, прокачка дивна за сучасними мірками, інвентар перевантажений сміттям і квестовими речами “а раптом знадобиться”. Але якщо не бігти вперед, а зупинятися і читати - гра починає розкриватися.

Найсильніше тут - дрібні деталі. Речі, які на початку здаються випадковими. Діалоги, в які можна повернутися і поставити нові питання про вже пережиті події. Предмети, що лежать півгри в інвентарі, а потім раптом знаходять сенс. Побічні історії, які несподівано вплітаються в основний сюжет. Світ не розділений на “головне” і “друге” - усе зшито в одну тканину пам’яті, провини і наслідків.

Десь у середині стає зрозуміло, до чого все йде. Інтрига не в тому, ЧИМ усе закінчиться, а в тому, ЧОМУ так сталося і КИМ ти був до цього. Фінал завжди один, хоч є трохи флейвору діалогах до нього, але немає слайдів про наслідки рішень. Спершу це трохи розчаровує. Потім розумієш: вся гра показана очима героя. Його історія завершується - світ продовжує рухатися без пояснень і без підсумкового звіту.

Окремо приємно, що гра має український переклад. Для проєкту, який живе текстом, це важливо. Бо без тексту цієї гри не існувало б. Механіки тут - оболонка. Це драматичний твір, розмазаний по світу, де історія ховається в розмовах, дослідженні та рефлексії.

Думаю, я подивлюся інші варіанти діалогів та подій через завантаження сейвів і навряд чи повернуся ще раз. І, мабуть, це правильно. Нехай залишиться це теперішнє відчуття захоплення від історії - а недоліки з часом згладяться... Забудуться.
